title: The saints next door
hook: Pope Francis wrote of holiness in ordinary people nearby
tomorrow: Year three close: the long story is yours

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sylvester, the pope whose feast ends the calendar year. Your line was the year's last saint. Today, the last day of saints across the calendar.

Since January you've walked the calendar: martyrs and popes, a monk in a boat, a girl with candles in her hair, an archbishop by an open door. Every one of them has a feast day and a statue somewhere. Now think of the woman two doors down who drives her neighbor to chemo every Tuesday. The grandfather who still prays before every meal, even in restaurants. The nurse on nights. None of them has a feast day. Does holiness need one?
screen: `A YEAR OF FEAST DAYS.` → `THE WOMAN TWO DOORS DOWN.` → `DOES HOLINESS NEED A FEAST?`

segments.voice: Start with Paul's letters. He doesn't write to a few heroes. He writes to whole congregations, people with jobs and worries and quarrels, and calls them saints. Philippians opens, in the Douay-Rheims, "to all the saints in Christ Jesus." The Greek word is hagioi, the holy ones, set apart for God. In Paul's letters it's simply what the ordinary baptized are called. Over the centuries the Church came to use the word in a narrower way too: those it formally declares to be in heaven, with a feast day and a place in the calendar. Both senses are alive in Catholic teaching. The Second Vatican Council spoke of a universal call to holiness: every Christian, not only priests and nuns. Pope Francis took that up in a letter on holiness, Gaudete et Exsultate, rejoice and be glad. He wrote about the saints next door, his phrase: parents raising their children with great love, men and women working hard to support their families, the sick, elderly religious who keep smiling. People living close to us, he wrote, who reflect God's presence. He warned against the idea that holiness means swooning in mystic rapture. For him, it often looks like small gestures: not gossiping, listening patiently, stopping to say a kind word to someone poor. So the calendar of this year isn't a list of a few superhumans with everybody else watching. It's a family album, and the Church says the album isn't finished.
screen: `PAUL CALLS WHOLE CHURCHES SAINTS.` · `A UNIVERSAL CALL TO HOLINESS.` · `THE SAINTS NEXT DOOR.` · `HOLINESS IN SMALL GESTURES.`

segments.voice: Let one face come to mind: someone whose goodness is quiet and steady, who will never be in a stained-glass window, a grandmother, a coworker, a neighbor, a friend in recovery. Remember one small thing they did that nobody else noticed. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if you don't, simply thank them in your heart.
hagioi. The Greek word, meaning the holy ones, that Paul used for the ordinary baptized, whole churches of saints, not only a few heroes. Today's word.
Your line: the saint next door. No feast day needed. One thousand sixty days now.

howItsDone: Catholics honor canonized saints on their feast days and also hold, with the Second Vatican Council, that every baptized person is called to holiness; on All Saints' Day the Church celebrates all the saints, including the holy ones no calendar names.

chat.says: Aren't saints just the famous ones with feast days and statues?
options: Those too, but Paul called whole churches saints, and all the baptized are called to holiness.
Yes, only those the Church declares in heaven can be called saints in any sense.
Yes, holiness is for a few heroes; the rest of us just watch and admire.
